doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Versatility and not being known as a jazz player
summary: He was called for any date, was an improviser rather than a known jazz player, and notes Jimmy Dorsey's difference.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well you got to be known as someone who could handle just about any kind of music that was put in front of you. You had that reputation.

Oh God yeah that’s a good question. You did call for a date and it didn’t matter what the date was. I didn’t get called so much for Dixieland or jazz, you know. I was not really known as a jazz player. I was an improviser. But you know the guy’s jealous — oh he doesn’t play like so-and-so, unless you sounded like Benny or Shaw you were no good. If you had your own style, you know. That’s why Jimmy Dorsey wasn’t too well known for his jazz clarinet playing, because he was different, he was entirely different.
